claims.text: The initial material is as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
Introducing controlled porosity can reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr without sacrificing its room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
The proposed intervention is the introduction of controlled porosity.
The intervention will produce a porous microstructure.
Controlled porosity reduces the overall density of the material.
A coherent high-entropy-alloy matrix will be retained after porosity is introduced.
Retention of a coherent high-entropy-alloy matrix will preserve strong mechanical properties despite the porosity.
The porous material will have lower density than as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The porous material will maintain, or only slightly reduce, yield strength at room temperature.
The porous material will maintain, or only slightly reduce, yield strength at temperatures up to 1000 °C.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g cm−3.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of about 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has an elevated-temperature yield strength of about 855 MPa.
The relevant temperature boundary is room temperature through 1000 °C.
Mechanical performance will be evaluated under uniaxial compression.
Porosity may be introduced by powder metallurgy or additive manufacturing.
A yield-strength reduction greater than 20% at either test temperature, without a corresponding density reduction, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires density reduction without sacrificing mechanical performance, whereas the predicted outcome permits a reduction in yield strength without defining how much reduction still counts as no sacrifice.

The falsification rule rejects a greater-than-20% strength loss only when no corresponding density reduction occurs. Thus, even a greater-than-20% strength loss would not falsify the hypothesis if density decreased, despite the stated requirement to avoid sacrificing performance.
